axis_note: S0 §3.1 lists this as a 'common ancestor' on the bio axis ('PAD (eLife) -- dreaming의 표현학습 역할'), feeding Part I module T6 (CLS theory and biological sleep). It is a computational neuroscience model, not an LLM paper: no language model, no tokens, no retrieval, no test-time adaptation appears anywhere in it. In the v2 three-layer frame it is nonetheless a genuine (U-E)-then-(U-Theta) system, which is why it can be reduced to the unified notation at all -- see update_layer.

problem_stated.statement: How do semantic cortical representations -- linearly separable, perturbation-invariant, object-identity-carrying activity in high visual areas -- emerge from unlabeled sensory experience, and what specifically do the two sleep states contribute to that emergence? The paper's own framing: 'Humans and other animals learn to extract general concepts from sensory experience without extensive teaching. This ability is thought to be facilitated by offline states like sleep where previous experiences are systemically replayed. However, the characteristic creative nature of dreams suggests that learning semantic representations may go beyond merely replaying previous experiences.' [Abstract, lines 11-14]
three_gaps_the_paper_names_in_prior_work: Helmholtz machine / Wake-Sleep line (Dayan et al. 1995; Hinton et al. 1995; Bornschein and Bengio 2015): 'these models do not leverage offline states to improve their generative model but are explicitly trained to reproduce sensory inputs during wakefulness' [lines 82-86]. Contrasted against the empirical fact that 'most dreams during REM sleep exhibit realistic imagery beyond past sensory experience' [line 85].

Cognitive 'trace transformation theory' (Nadel and Moscovitch 1997; Winocur et al. 2010; Lewis and Durrant 2011): 'these models lack a mechanistic implementation compatible with cortical structures and only consider the replay of waking activity during sleep' [lines 87-89].

Existing functional theories of dreaming (creative problem solving, prospective coding, complexity minimization; Cai et al. 2009; Llewellyn 2015/2016; Hobson et al. 2014; Hoel 2021): 'these theories do not consider the role of dreams for a more basic function, such as the formation of semantic cortical representations' [lines 104-105].
problem_stated.hypothesis: 'we propose that dreams, and in particular their creative combination of episodic memories, play an essential role in forming semantic representations over the course of development' [lines 106-107]. Mechanistically: 'generating new but realistic sensory experiences, instead of merely reconstructing previous observations, requires the brain to understand the composition of its sensorium' [lines 113-115].
problem_stated.claimed_result: 'generating new, virtual sensory inputs via adversarial dreaming during REM sleep is essential for extracting semantic concepts, while replaying episodic memories via perturbed dreaming during NREM sleep improves the robustness of latent representations' [Abstract, lines 17-20].
problem_stated.source: Abstract lines 11-21; Introduction lines 55-121; Results opening lines 184-193

inherited_open_question.detail: The paper quotes no prior author's stated open question and has no sentence of the form 'X et al. left open whether ...'. Every lineage statement is the authors' own characterization of a prior literature's limit (the three quoted in problem_stated.three_gaps_the_paper_names_in_prior_work). Per S0 §4 this absence is itself recorded rather than papered over.
inherited_open_question.what_it_implicitly_answers: It answers a question that the Wake-Sleep / Helmholtz line posed only structurally and never in words: if the offline phase is where the generative pathway is trained, what objective should the offline phase optimize? Wake-Sleep answers 'reconstruct the input, using dreams only as a source of (z, x) pairs to fit the recognition model'. PAD answers 'make the dream indistinguishable from waking input, and train the generative pathway ADVERSARIALLY during the offline state itself'. The paper states the contrast in exactly these terms, but as a testable prediction rather than as an inherited question: 'in alternative representation learning models that involve offline states such as the Wake-Sleep algorithm (Hinton et al., 1995), generative pathways are not trained to produce realistic dreams during the sleep phase. Rather, they are trained by reconstruction on real input data during the wake phase.' [lines 1155-1157]
inherited_open_question.second_implicit_inheritance: From the cognitive-science side it supplies the mechanism that trace-transformation theory lacked ('lack a mechanistic implementation compatible with cortical structures' [line 88]) -- but again as the authors' diagnosis, not as a quoted question.
inherited_open_question.bridge_in_material_for_the_monograph: Because there is no inherited quote, the chapter's §N.1 must open from the community gap rather than from a predecessor's future-work paragraph: the CLS/replay tradition (McClelland et al. 1995, cited at line 945) says sleep replays what happened; the dream phenomenology (Fosse et al. 2003, cited at line 85) says REM dreams are NOT what happened. PAD is the first functional model to take the second fact as the computational primitive instead of as noise.
inherited_open_question.note_writer_flag: The absence is a real finding about the relationship between the bio axis and the LLM axes: this paper's open questions were never picked up in words by the LLM sleep-time line either -- see cross_path_citations.

core_mechanism.one_line: One cycle k writes the encoder's latent for the current mini-batch into a two-slot hippocampal buffer -- that is (U-E) with a degenerate query-free write -- and then runs (U-Theta) three times with three different outer losses on three different self-generated training sets: real inputs at Wake, single-memory replays rendered through the generator and occluded at NREM, and noise-diluted convex mixtures of two memories rendered through the generator at REM, where the generator's gradient sign is inverted so that the offline phase trains the generative pathway adversarially against a discriminator head on the encoder.

layer_assignment.Theta: the slow weights of this paper are the union of the encoder/discriminator parameters and the generator parameters: Theta = (Theta^{enc}, Theta^{disc}, Theta^{gen}), the paper's theta_E and theta_G [Algorithm 1, line 1287]. Every plasticity event in the paper moves Theta.
layer_assignment.W: EMPTY. There are no fast weights, no test-time state, no inner loss, no inner learning rate. The reader must be told this explicitly: at evaluation the model is a single frozen forward pass. 'While training the classifier, the connectivity of the network (E and G) is fixed.' [lines 531-532]
layer_assignment.E: the hippocampal module. 'As a detailed hippocampus model is outside the scope of this study, we mimic hippocampal storage and retrieval by storing and reading latent representations to and from memory.' [lines 1262-1263]. Its contents are the latent mini-batches Z (this cycle) and Z_old (previous cycle) [Algorithm 1, lines 1351, 1423].

core_mechanism.cycle_summary_in_paper_words: 'each Wake-NREM-REM cycle consists of (1) reconstructing a mini-batch x of images during Wake, (2) reconstructing a mini-batch of latent activities Z = E_z(X) during NREM with perturbation of G(z), and (3) replaying Z convex combined with Z_old and noise from the (n-1)th cycle. In PAD training, all losses are weighted equally and we did not use a schedule for L_KL, as opposed to standard variational autoencoder training.' [lines 1618-1621]

architecture.encoder_E_z: four convolutional layers with 64, 128, 256, 256 channels; 4x4 kernel, padding 1 (0 for last layer), stride 2 (feature size halved per layer); LeakyReLU on all but the last layer; the last conv layer's activity IS z [lines 1250-1253]
architecture.discriminator_head_E_d: one additional convolutional layer plus sigmoid, attached to the SECOND-TO-LAST layer of the encoder, mapping to a single scalar d with putative teaching signal 0 or 1; E_z and E_d share the first three convolutional layers [lines 1253-1257]
architecture.generator_G: four deconvolutional layers with 256, 128, 64, 3 channels; 4x4 kernel, padding 1 (0 for the first deconvolutional layer), stride 2 (feature size doubled per layer); LeakyReLU on the first three, tanh on the last [lines 1258-1261]
architecture.deliberately_absent: 'in contrast to previous GAN variants, our model removes many optimization tricks such as batch normalization layers, spectral normalization layers, or optimizing the min-max GAN objective in three steps with different objectives, which are challenging to implement in biological substrates' [lines 997-1000]

outer_vs_inner.reader_note: This paper has NO inner loop. Nothing moves at query time. Every learnable object below is moved by gradient descent between mini-batches, i.e. by (U-Theta) at the sleep-round timescale k. The only 'wake-time movement' in the whole paper is the write of one latent vector into a two-slot buffer, which involves no learning at all.

rows.when: ALL THREE PHASES of every cycle k. Wake: on calL_img + calL_KL + calL_real. NREM: on calL_nrem (this is the only thing NREM trains). REM: on calL_rem (descent).

rows.object: discriminator head (1 conv + sigmoid on the encoder's second-to-last layer; shares the first three conv layers with the encoder)
rows.who_learns: outer-loop gradient descent, jointly with the encoder because the parameters are shared up to layer 3
rows.when: Wake (target 'external' = 1) and REM (target 'internal' = 0). Not trained during NREM: 'the state-specific modulation provides a high activity target for the discriminator during Wake, which is decreased during REM and entirely gated off during NREM' [lines 866-868].

rows.who_learns: outer-loop gradient DESCENT at Wake on calL_img only; outer-loop gradient ASCENT at REM on calL_rem
rows.when: Wake and REM. NOT updated during NREM -- Algorithm 1 has no theta_G line in the NREM block [lines 1359-1377]. 'An oblique arrow indicates that learning occurs in a given pathway' [Figure 2 caption, line 263]; 'The red minus on G indicates the inverted plasticity implementing this adversarial training' [Figure 2 caption, lines 270-271].

rows.who_learns: nobody -- it is a WRITE, not a learning step. wr is a copy of the encoder output.
rows.when: WAKE-TIME MOVEMENT. Written once per cycle, read during NREM (as target) and REM (as one term of the mixture).

rows.who_learns: nobody -- shifted in at the END of the REM phase ('Z_old <- Z // keep current vectors for next iteration')
rows.when: written at the end of cycle k, read during cycle k+1's REM only. Retention is exactly ONE cycle.
REM only. Contributes half the latent mixture at lambda' = 0.5.

rows.who_learns: nobody -- sampled per mini-batch. Two parameters are drawn: occlusion probability uniformly between 0 and 1, and square size between 1 and 8.
rows.when: NREM only. 'For each mini-batch, a probability and square size were randomly picked between 0 and 1, and 1-8, respectively.' [lines 1627-1628]
rows.source: Methods 'Image occlusion' lines 1625-1629; Eq. 6; Figure 9 lines 1594-1596

rows.who_learns: nobody -- fixed hyperparameters, stated once and never varied

rows.object: linear readout (evaluation probe, NOT part of the model)
rows.who_learns: supervised SGD with labels, eta_ro = 0.2, b = 64, 20 epochs over the whole training set
rows.when: AFTER the model is frozen, once per measured epoch. 'While training the classifier, the connectivity of the network (E and G) is fixed.' [lines 531-532]. The paper flags this as a modelling assumption it does not defend: 'In its current form, PAD assumes that training the linear readout does not lead to weight changes in the encoder network.' [lines 1042-1043]

rows.object: the 'conductor' that supplies the discriminator's teaching signal (external!/internal!)
rows.who_learns: nobody -- it is a POSTULATED brain-state signal, not an implemented component. 'It also postulates a conductor that orchestrates learning by providing a teaching (nudging) signal to the discriminator neurons during Wake and REM.' [lines 855-856]
rows.when: in the simulation this is simply the hard-coded constant target 1 at Wake and 0 at REM.

outer_vs_inner.what_moves_at_query_time: Nothing. hat-y = W_ro enc(x). There is no retrieval, no state update, no adaptation. Every benefit claimed by the paper has already been amortized into Theta^{enc} before the query arrives -- which is precisely the shape S0 §2.3 defines as sleep-time compute, with the difference that here B_s is spent on gradient steps rather than on inference.

update_layer.instantiates: (U-E) then (U-Theta), (U-Theta) -- in that order, three times per cycle k, with three different outer losses.
order_within_one_cycle_k: 1. WAKE, (U-E): hat-c_k = enc(x_k) is written into the two-slot store. S(.;B_s) is a single encoder forward pass -- the cheapest possible instance of the (U-E) write.

2. WAKE, (U-Theta): Theta moves on calL_wake = calL_img + calL_KL + calL_real, using REAL data. R_k here is the actual mini-batch, not a generated set. This step is not sleep-time compute at all; it is ordinary online learning.
3. NREM, (U-Theta): R_k = {(gen_pix(hat-c)⊙omega, hat-c)} is built entirely from the store plus the generator. Only Theta^{enc} moves.
4. REM, (U-Theta): R_k = {(gen_pix(z^mix), 'internal')} where z^mix mixes the two stored slots with N(0,I) noise at 1/4 : 1/4 : 1/2. Theta^{disc} descends, Theta^{gen} ASCENDS.
differences_from_canonical_U_Theta: Canonical (U-Theta) has ONE outer loss calL. PAD has three, selected by a global brain-state variable: 'the three brain states only differ in their objective function and the presence or absence of external input' [lines 275-276]. The chapter should present the phase as an argument to calL, i.e. calL^{(phase)}(R_k; Theta_k).

Canonical (U-Theta) is gradient DESCENT. The REM block on Theta^{gen} is gradient ASCENT on the same loss: Theta^{gen} <- Theta^{gen} + eta_Theta grad calL_rem [Algorithm 1, line 1421]. The canonical form cannot express this without an explicit sign field. This is not a technicality -- it is the paper's headline biological prediction (Figure 7 'sign switch', lines 813-815).

Canonical R_k = gen(H_k; B_s) presumes an experience history H_k. Here H_k is TWO mini-batches of latents and nothing else. The rest of the 'experience' has already been absorbed into Theta and is unrecoverable. So the store is a working buffer, not a history.

In NREM the store supplies the TARGETS and the generator supplies the INPUTS. In an ordinary replay scheme (see deep-generative-replay note) the generator supplies inputs and a frozen teacher supplies targets. PAD inverts which side of the pair is authoritative: the stored latent is treated as ground truth about 'what this experience was'.

In REM the target is not a stored quantity at all: it is the constant label 'internal'. So this (U-Theta) round consumes ZERO information from the store's contents in its target; the store only shapes the input distribution.
differences_from_canonical_U_E: wr(.) is a plain copy; there is no summarization, compaction, dedup or scoring. S(c_k; B_s) costs one encoder forward pass.

There is NO ret(E, q). Reads are by round index (current slot, previous slot), never by query. In the v2 path catalogue this makes PAD an E-path system with the retrieval half amputated -- the store exists solely to feed (U-Theta).
C_cap is bounded at 2 slots by construction: 'Z_old <- Z' overwrites [Algorithm 1, line 1423]. Retention is one cycle. Nothing in the paper accumulates.
not_instantiated: (U-W): completely absent. No fast weights, no test-time state, no inner loss, no inner learning rate, no chunking. The chapter must say this in one sentence so the reader does not go looking.
update_layer.path_verdict: Under S0 §1.6's discriminant, PAD executes (U-E) AND (U-Theta), so it is not a pure member of any single path; it is the common ancestor in which the two are not yet separated. That is exactly why S0 §3.1 files it as a 공통조상 rather than under E/W/Theta.
